riskToHumans.metaTitle: Risk to humans — what harmless, moderate, and high mean
riskToHumans.metaDescription: Georgia’s reptiles are labelled harmless, moderate, or high risk to people. What each level means, which species it covers, and what to do if you meet one.
riskToHumans.keywords: risk to humans, snake risk Georgia, venomous snakes Georgia, high risk viper, moderate risk, harmless snakes, Macrovipera lebetina, risk levels reptiles
riskToHumans.title: Risk to humans
riskToHumans.subtitle: This atlas uses three labels: harmless, moderate, and high. Here is what each one means — and what to do if you meet the animal.
riskToHumans.scaleTitle: A field label, not a medical diagnosis
riskToHumans.scaleLead: The badge on a species page is this atlas’s classification of medical risk to people in Georgia. It is not a lab ranking of venom potency, not a measure of how “aggressive” the animal is, and not the same as conservation status.
riskToHumans.scaleDisclaimer: Educational page — not emergency medical advice. If bitten, call 112.
riskToHumans.scaleHighBody: A bite can cause severe local and systemic illness. Keep distance. If bitten, this is an emergency.
riskToHumans.scaleModerateBody: Venomous, with a lower typical profile than the highest-risk vipers — a bite still needs medical care.
riskToHumans.scaleHarmlessBody: Most species here. No medically significant venom. Do not pick them up anyway — handling stresses the animal and can confuse lookalikes.
riskToHumans.HighLead: In this atlas, high risk means a medically serious bite: local tissue damage and possible systemic effects that need hospital care. These are not animals that hunt people. Most bites happen when someone tries to catch, kill, or move the snake.
riskToHumans.HighPoint1Body: Two vipers: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetina) — Georgia’s largest venomous snake, with the highest typical venom yield — and the Transcaucasian long-nosed viper (Vipera transcaucasiana). Both can cause a life-threatening bite.
riskToHumans.HighPoint2Body: Do not handle it. Step back or go around. Even for a photo, do not close in. The snake will usually leave if it has a way out.
riskToHumans.HighPoint3Body: Call 112 immediately. Stay as still as you can and do not move the bitten limb. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet. This page does not replace a clinician.
riskToHumans.HighSpeciesBody: Open a profile for identification, range, and encounter notes.
riskToHumans.ModerateLead: Venomous, and a bite is a medical event — but the typical outcome is assessed below the two high-risk vipers. “Moderate” is not “mild”: it still means keep distance and get care after a bite.
riskToHumans.ModeratePoint1Body: Four Vipera — Caucasus, Dinnik’s, Darevsky’s, and steppe — plus one rear-fanged species, the eastern Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus). The rear-fanged bite is usually milder; it should still be taken seriously.
riskToHumans.ModeratePoint2Body: The same rule as for high risk: do not pick it up, do not corner it, do not try to move it. Distance settles most encounters.
riskToHumans.ModeratePoint3Body: Call 112. A moderate-risk bite can still cause painful swelling and needs a medical assessment. Do not wait to “see if it gets worse.”
riskToHumans.ModerateSpeciesBody: Vipers first, then the rear-fanged species. Each profile states why the risk sits here and not higher.
riskToHumans.HarmlessLead: No medically significant venom. This is the default for lizards, turtles, amphibians, and most snakes in Georgia. Harmless does not mean “pick it up” — and it does not mean the animal never bites if handled.
riskToHumans.HarmlessPoint1Body: A bite from these species is not a venom emergency. Several harmless snakes flatten the head or hiss so they look like a viper. Identification belongs on the species page, not in the hand.
riskToHumans.HarmlessPoint2Body: Watch it and leave it where it is. Handling stresses the animal, can spread disease in amphibians, and leaves a risk of confusing a viper for a lookalike.
riskToHumans.HarmlessPoint3Body: Wash your hands. Amphibian skin produces mucus or defensive secretions; moving animals between ponds spreads fungal disease. A hard bite from a large harmless snake is still a wound — clean it, and seek care if it needs stitches.
riskToHumans.HarmlessSpeciesBody: Grass snakes, the smooth snake, the cat snake, and the glass lizard are the mix-ups this atlas sees most. The rest of the harmless catalog is in the atlas filter.

riskToHumans.faqIntro: Short answers on the three-level scale. Full species detail lives on each profile.
riskToHumans.faq1Q: What does the badge on a species page mean?
riskToHumans.faq1A: It is this atlas’s label for medical risk to people: harmless, moderate, or high. Clicking it opens this page, scrolled to that level. It is not IUCN status and not a score for how likely the animal is to approach you.
riskToHumans.faq2Q: Does “harmless” mean it will not bite?
riskToHumans.faq2A: No. Harmless means no medically significant venom. A large colubrid can still bite hard if handled. Several harmless snakes mimic vipers when threatened. Leave the animal where it is.
riskToHumans.faq3Q: Why is the Montpellier snake moderate if it is not a viper?
riskToHumans.faq3A: Malpolon insignitus is rear-fanged, not a viper. Risk to people is usually milder than a viper bite, but it is still medically relevant in this atlas — treat a bite seriously and call 112.
riskToHumans.faq4Q: Which snakes are high risk in Georgia?
riskToHumans.faq4A: Two: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetina) and the Transcaucasian long-nosed viper (Vipera transcaucasiana). Other vipers in the atlas are moderate. A bite from any of them needs medical care.
riskToHumans.faq5Q: Are lizards, turtles, or amphibians ever high risk?
riskToHumans.faq5A: Not in this atlas. Venom risk to people applies to certain snakes. Lizards, turtles, and amphibians are labelled harmless. Do not pick them up; wash hands after any contact.

seo.title: How the regional atlas works
seo.p1: In Georgia, reptile assemblages shift with place: Colchic forests and the western coast, the Greater Caucasus high belt, and the arid basins of the east each support different species. The regional atlas turns that gradient into a practical path — pick a place on the map or in the list and see what is recorded there.
seo.p2: Each region page brings together confirmed species lists, habitats, venomous-snake notes, and a map. Amphibians, turtles, and almost all lizards (except the glass lizard) are not mapped yet — that is a gap, not a complete fauna. The full snake regional view is also on the range guide.

seo.reptilesP1: Georgia sits between the Black Sea, the Greater Caucasus, and the arid east — a short geographic span that supports vipers of high mountains and Colchic forests, water snakes of rivers and wetlands, racers of dry foothills, and a widespread legless lizard often mistaken for a snake. Reptile profiles here are bilingual, with Georgia-specific range notes and field photography.
seo.reptilesP2: Species richness here is shaped by elevation, humidity, and refuge habitats. Western Colchic landscapes favor moisture-linked snakes such as Natrix; eastern semi-arid basins hold Macrovipera lebetina and fast colubrids; alpine and subalpine belts hold Caucasus endemics including Vipera dinniki. This section is about reptiles — snakes, lizards, and turtles.
seo.amphibiansP1: Frogs, toads, newts, and the Caucasian salamander sit in the same catalog, with dedicated guides. This is not a complete national list — only published profiles.
seo.birdsP1: Bird profiles follow the same rule: named sources, no invented maps. The list is growing and does not replace the national avifauna checklist.
seo.mammalsP1: Mammal pages use the same profile structure. Few are published yet — absence from this catalog does not mean the species is absent from Georgia.
seo.venomousP1: Only a minority of Georgia’s snakes are medically significant. In this atlas, “venomous” means moderate or high risk to humans: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetina), Caucasus viper (Vipera kaznakovi), Dinnik’s viper (Vipera dinniki), Transcaucasian long-nosed viper (Vipera transcaucasiana), Darevsky’s viper (Vipera darevskii), and steppe viper (Vipera renardi). Most other snakes here — grass snake, dice snake, racers, smooth snake, cat snake — are harmless to people, though several are frequently misidentified.
seo.venomousP2: Safe encounter practice is simple: do not handle wild snakes, keep distance, and learn the lookalikes common in your region. Open each profile for identification traits, habitat, and conservation status. This is educational natural-history guidance, not emergency medical advice.
seo.venomousGuideCta: Full guide: venomous snakes in Georgia
seo.regionsP1: Distribution in the atlas is recorded by Georgia’s administrative regions as a practical field layer — from Abkhazia and Adjara on the humid west to Kakheti and Kvemo Kartli in the dry east, plus the capital district of Tbilisi. A species may appear in several regions; endemics and elevational specialists are more narrowly placed.
seo.regionsP2: Use the map to move from place to fauna, then open regional pages for habitats, safety notes, and the local species list. For research-grade occurrence data, profiles also cite databases such as GBIF and the Reptile Database alongside IUCN assessments where available.

venomousSnakes.safetyTitle: What to do if you meet one
venomousSnakes.safetyLead: Most vipers will not strike unless they feel threatened. Distance and calm usually settle the encounter.
venomousSnakes.safetyDisclaimer: This page is educational and is not emergency medical instruction. If bitten, call 112.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep1Body: Never catch or move a wild snake — most bites happen during handling.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep2Body: Pass aside or back away. Even for a photo, do not close in.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep3Body: Many harmless snakes resemble vipers. Killing by mistake harms the ecosystem.
venomousSnakes.safetyStep4Body: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm and do not move the bitten arm or leg. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet. This does not replace a doctor’s advice.

venomousSnakes.faq1Q: How many venomous snakes are there in Georgia?
venomousSnakes.faq1A: This atlas treats six vipers as medically significant: the Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetinus), Transcaucasian long-nosed viper, Caucasus viper, Dinnik’s viper, Darevsky’s viper, and steppe viper. In addition, the eastern Montpellier snake (Malpolon insignitus) is a moderate-risk rear-fanged species — not a viper.
venomousSnakes.faq2Q: Which venomous snake is the most dangerous?
venomousSnakes.faq2A: The Levantine viper (Macrovipera lebetina) is Georgia’s largest and most dangerous venomous snake; its bite can threaten human life. The Transcaucasian long-nosed viper is also high risk; the Caucasus, Dinnik’s, Darevsky’s, and steppe vipers are assessed as moderate risk.
venomousSnakes.faq3Q: Where do venomous snakes occur in Georgia?
venomousSnakes.faq3A: The Levantine viper favors dry rocky east; the Caucasus viper Colchic forests and the western coast; Dinnik’s viper the high Greater Caucasus; the Transcaucasian long-nosed viper the Meskheti–Trialeti ranges; Darevsky’s viper the Javakheti–Erusheti highlands; the steppe viper Javakheti plateaus and eastern steppes. Exact regions are on each species profile and in the regional atlas.
venomousSnakes.faq4Q: How do I tell a venomous snake from a harmless one?
venomousSnakes.faq4A: Vipers often have a vertical pupil and a more triangular head; many harmless snakes have a round pupil. The rule is not foolproof — learn species traits and habitat from the profiles instead.
venomousSnakes.faq5Q: What should I do if bitten?
venomousSnakes.faq5A: Seek medical care immediately. Stay calm, do not move the bitten arm or leg, and avoid home remedies (cutting, sucking, tourniquets). This page is educational and does not replace a clinician.

snakeBite.disclaimerNote: Only medical staff decide treatment. The steps here are educational first-response points based on WHO, CDC, and 112 public guidance — not an antivenom protocol.
snakeBite.doTitle: What to do after a snakebite
snakeBite.do1Body: Immediately. 112 is Georgia’s single emergency number — police, fire, and ambulance. Do not wait for symptoms.
snakeBite.do2Body: Get to a safe place. Do not approach the animal again, and do not try to catch or kill it.
snakeBite.do3Body: Sit or lie down somewhere safe and limit unnecessary movement until help arrives.
snakeBite.do4Title: Keep the bitten limb as still as you can
snakeBite.do4Body: Keep the bitten arm or leg as still as possible. This is educational guidance — not a full clinical protocol.
snakeBite.do5Body: Rings, watches, bracelets, or tight clothing near the bite can cause harm if swelling develops.
snakeBite.do6Body: Home remedies do not replace medical care. If possible, do not drive yourself — symptoms can affect you.
snakeBite.dont1Body: Cutting or excising the wound does not remove venom and causes harm.
snakeBite.dont2Body: Sucking venom by mouth or device does not work and damages the wound.
snakeBite.dont3Body: A tight arterial tourniquet is not recommended for snakebite and can cause serious harm.
snakeBite.dont4Title: Do not catch or handle the snake
snakeBite.dont4Body: Catching a snake — even a dead one — often causes another bite. Identification from a distance or a photo is enough, and only if safe.
snakeBite.dont5Title: Do not use alcohol or folk remedies
snakeBite.dont5Body: Alcohol, ice, electric shock, or other unproven methods are not treatment and waste time.
snakeBite.dont6Title: Do not delay care to identify the species
snakeBite.dont6Body: Call 112 and seek care first. Species ID must not delay the emergency call.
snakeBite.symptomsIntro: Symptoms vary with species, venom, bite location, amount of venom, and other factors. The list below is possible signs — not a diagnostic checklist.
snakeBite.symptomsUrgent: Do not wait for symptoms before calling 112. Absence of symptoms does not mean the bite is safe.
snakeBite.symptomsNote: Local and general signs mainly follow the CDC public list; serious effects of envenoming follow the WHO fact sheet. The list is not complete. For severe or unusual symptoms, call 112.
snakeBite.dangerTitle: When is a snakebite especially dangerous?
snakeBite.dangerIntro: Every suspected bite is an emergency for 112. Below are situations that need especially fast response.
snakeBite.danger1: Difficulty breathing, severe swelling, or systemic symptoms.
snakeBite.danger2: Children often experience more severe effects because of smaller body mass.
snakeBite.danger3: Delaying care increases risk — do not postpone transport to a health facility.
snakeBite.danger4: If you did not see the snake but suspect a bite — still seek emergency care.
snakeBite.venomBody: No. Many snakes in Georgia are not venomous to people, though a bite can still cause injury or infection. The atlas lists <venomous>venomous species</venomous> whose bites are medically important. Species comparison belongs in the <identify>identification guide</identify>, not at the bite scene.
snakeBite.venomNote: Do not try to judge medical risk yourself. That decision belongs to medical staff.
snakeBite.unseenEyebrow: If you did not see the snake
snakeBite.unseenTitle: What if I did not see the snake?
snakeBite.unseenBody: Still call 112 and seek emergency care. Do not delay the call to identify the species. If you can observe safely from a distance or take a photo, that may help later — never approach or catch the animal.
snakeBite.unseenId: Species comparison later — in the <identify>venomous snake ID guide</identify>, only after emergency care is underway.
snakeBite.sourcesTitle: What this page is based on
snakeBite.sourcesIntro: Medical recommendations cite external authoritative sources. Species and range information come from the Reptiles.ge atlas. This page is not an independent medical authority.
snakeBite.sourceExt1Body: Georgia’s single emergency number. After a bite, this is the first action.
snakeBite.sourceExt2Body: Move away from the bite area, remove tight items, immobilize; avoid tight arterial tourniquets, wound incision/excision, venom suction, and traditional methods; transport promptly to a health facility.
snakeBite.sourceExt3Body: Possible effects of envenoming: paralysis, bleeding disorders, tissue damage; children may experience more severe effects.
snakeBite.sourceExt4Title: CDC / NIOSH — Venomous snakes first aid
snakeBite.sourceExt4Body: Emergency care without waiting for symptoms; remove rings/watches; do not cut, suck, or tourniquet; do not catch the snake; do not drink alcohol.

snakeBite.faqIntro: Short answers for an urgent situation. Detail is above; medical decisions belong with 112 and clinicians.
snakeBite.ctaBody: Species comparison and prevention live on profiles and guides. After a bite, 112 still comes first.
snakeBite.faq1Q: What should I do first after a snakebite?
snakeBite.faq1A: Call 112 immediately — do not wait for symptoms. Move away from the snake, limit movement, and keep the bitten limb still. Do not cut, suck, or apply a tourniquet.
snakeBite.faq2A: No. WHO and CDC rule out cutting the wound — it causes harm.
snakeBite.faq3Q: Can I suck out the venom?
snakeBite.faq3A: No. Sucking venom does not work and damages the wound.
snakeBite.faq4A: No. A tight arterial tourniquet is not recommended for snakebite.
snakeBite.faq5A: No. Many snakes are non-venomous, though a bite can still injure. Do not judge risk yourself — call 112.
snakeBite.faq6Q: What symptoms can a snakebite cause?
snakeBite.faq6A: Pain, swelling, bleeding, weakness, nausea, breathing difficulty, or neurological signs may occur. Absence of symptoms does not mean safety.
snakeBite.faq7Q: Should I catch the snake so doctors know the species?
snakeBite.faq7A: No. Catching it often causes another bite. A distant look or photo is enough if safe.
snakeBite.faq8Q: What if I did not see the snake?
snakeBite.faq8A: Still call 112. Do not delay the call for identification. Species comparison can wait.

turtleIdentify.metaTitle: Turtle identification — how to tell Georgia’s turtles apart
turtleIdentify.metaDescription: Identify turtles in Georgia: land or water, slider or native, pond turtle or Caspian — a four-species field key with photos and diagnostics.

turtleIdentify.title: Turtle identification in Georgia — what turtle is this?
turtleIdentify.subtitle: Start with a few clear field marks: land or water, shell shape, head and neck. The key below narrows to four atlas checklist options — open a profile afterward to confirm and go deeper.
turtleIdentify.guideP1: The atlas checklist has four turtles: one land tortoise (Testudo graeca), two native freshwater turtles (Emys orbicularis, Mauremys caspica), and one introduced slider (Trachemys scripta). Below is a photo-backed decision path.
turtleIdentify.guideP2: The full table and empty fields live in the <index>turtle species index</index>. This page is for identification, not the catalog.
turtleIdentify.flowTitle: How to identify a turtle in Georgia
turtleIdentify.flowBody: Start with where you saw it. Then, for water turtles, check for a red ear stripe. If that mark is absent, compare the pond turtle and the Caspian turtle.
turtleIdentify.step1Title: Step 1 — where did you see it?
turtleIdentify.step1Body: Walking on open, dry ground with a high dome — land branch. Pond, lake, marsh, or basking on a bank — water branch.
turtleIdentify.branchLandBody: High domed shell, columnar unwebbed legs, slow walking on dry or open ground.
turtleIdentify.branchLandAlt: Spur-thighed tortoise with a high domed shell on land
turtleIdentify.branchWaterBody: Flatter shell, webbed feet; pond, lake, marsh, or basking on the bank.
turtleIdentify.branchWaterAlt: Freshwater turtle with a flatter shell by water
turtleIdentify.landResultBody: Georgia’s only land tortoise. Separated from water turtles by the dome, columnar legs, and often thigh spurs.
turtleIdentify.step2Title: Step 2 — water turtle: red mark behind the eye?
turtleIdentify.step2Body: T. s. elegans has a broad red or orange stripe behind the eye. If that mark is clear — introduced slider. If not — compare the two native freshwater turtles.
turtleIdentify.branchSliderBody: Broad red stripe behind the eye, flatter shell; often in city ponds near Tbilisi and Batumi.
turtleIdentify.branchSliderAlt: Red-eared slider — broad red stripe behind the eye
turtleIdentify.branchNativeBody: Native freshwater turtles: European pond turtle (Emys) or Caspian turtle (Mauremys). Side-by-side comparison below.
turtleIdentify.branchNativeAlt: Native water turtle without a red ear stripe
turtleIdentify.sliderResultBody: An introduced species; wild populations are confirmed near Tbilisi and Batumi. Not native.
turtleIdentify.emysVsTitle: Pond turtle or Caspian turtle — how to tell them apart
turtleIdentify.emysVsBody: Both are native freshwater turtles and lack the slider’s red ear stripe. Below are the most useful field marks for telling them apart.
turtleIdentify.emysVsEmysCaption: Often a dark shell with yellow dots; head and neck dark with dots or short streaks.
turtleIdentify.emysVsMauremysCaption: Pale lengthwise neck stripes often present; shell usually more striped than speckled.

emys.shell: Low, oval; usually dark olive, brown, or black; often yellow dots or streaks.
emys.headNeck: Dark head, neck, and legs with yellow dots or short streaks; no red ear stripe.
emys.plastron: Paler plastron; Emys has a movable hinge.
emys.habitat: Freshwater ponds, lakes, and marshes; webbed feet; often basks on banks.
emys.range: Western and eastern Georgia (per profile); the map does not yet fully shade eastern regions.

mauremys.shell: Flatter than a land-tortoise dome; usually more striped than speckled.
mauremys.headNeck: Pale lengthwise neck stripes often present; no red ear stripe.

snakesInYard.metaTitle: How to get snakes out of the yard — what works and what doesn’t
snakesInYard.metaDescription: Snakes in the yard: there is no 100% snake repellent. Reduce shelter and food so snakes do not stay. What works in Georgia — and which myths waste your time.
snakesInYard.keywords: how to get rid of snakes in the yard, snakes in yard, snake repellent, snake in garden, sulfur snake myth, milk for snakes, Georgia snakes yard
snakesInYard.heroImageAlt: A specialist safely capturing a snake in a residential yard with professional tongs
snakesInYard.title: How to get snakes out of the yard
snakesInYard.subtitle: There is no reliable way to “drive them out” on command. Make the yard poor for shelter and food — then a snake will not stay.
snakesInYard.whyTitle: Why do snakes enter a yard?
snakesInYard.whyLead: No method repels snakes with 100% effect. A yard usually attracts them for two reasons — shelter and food.
snakesInYard.whyShelterBody: Tall grass, shrubs, logs, stones, building materials, and wall cracks make good cover.
snakesInYard.whyFoodBody: Rodents are prey for many snakes. If mice or rats thrive in the yard, conditions improve for snakes too.
snakesInYard.coverImageAlt: A snake on rocks near rodents and tall grass — shelter and food in one place
snakesInYard.coverCaption: A yard attracts snakes when it offers shelter (rocks, logs, tall grass) and food (rodents).
snakesInYard.actionsTitle: What to do so they stop coming in
snakesInYard.actionsLead: The goal is not to kill or catch a snake — it is to manage the yard so neither shelter nor food remains.
snakesInYard.action1Title: Regular clearing of grass in the yard
snakesInYard.action1Body: Cut tall grass — the area becomes more open and less attractive to snakes.
snakesInYard.action2Body: Fill burrows and holes, reduce dense shrubs along edges, seal cracks in walls, and clear logs, stones, and building materials from the yard — snakes often hide there.
snakesInYard.action3Body: Rodents are food for snakes. If mice or rats are present, address that first — conditions for snakes worsen on their own.
snakesInYard.mythsLead: These methods are often recommended, but they have no reliable effect. Spend time and money on yard management instead.
snakesInYard.appearTitle: What to do if a snake is in the yard
snakesInYard.appearBody: Do not try to catch or kill it — that is dangerous and often targets a harmless species. Watch from a distance, leave an exit open, and call the right service when you need help.
snakesInYard.contactBiteBody: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm, do not move the bitten arm or leg, and avoid home remedies (cutting, sucking, tourniquets).
snakesInYard.contactAgencyBody: Call them — they can help catch the reptile safely. Do not attempt it yourself.
snakesInYard.faqIntro: Short answers — practice is above; species detail lives in the atlas.
snakesInYard.faq1Q: Is there a product that repels snakes 100%?
snakesInYard.faq1A: No. The most effective approach is reducing shelter and food. Repellent sprays, sulfur, and similar methods do not deliver reliable results. Even after yard management, one may still appear — but it will not stay.
snakesInYard.faq2Q: Why do snakes come into the yard?
snakesInYard.faq2A: Mainly for shelter and food. Tall grass, logs, stones, building materials, and rodents make a yard more attractive.
snakesInYard.faq3Q: Do milk, sulfur, or sprays work?
snakesInYard.faq3A: No — these are common myths. Yard management works better: cut grass, remove shelter, and control rodents.
snakesInYard.faq4Q: What if a snake is already in the yard?
snakesInYard.faq4A: Do not touch it or try to catch it. Watch from a distance and leave an exit. If you need the snake removed safely, call the Animal Monitoring Agency: 032 272 16 00.
snakesInYard.faq5Q: What if a snake bites someone?
snakesInYard.faq5A: Call 112 immediately. Stay calm, do not move the bitten arm or leg, and do not use home remedies (cutting, sucking, tourniquets). This page is educational and does not replace medical advice.
snakesInYard.faq6A: No. In Georgia, non-venomous species are more common and are often confused with vipers. Compare profiles in the atlas before acting out of fear.
snakesInYard.ctaTitle: Identify the species — don’t act on fear alone
snakesInYard.ctaBody: Yard management lowers risk. If you see a snake, the atlas helps with identification and a safer decision.

snakeQuiz.practiceTitle: How to read a snake in a still frame
snakeQuiz.practiceLead: This page is a quiz, not a field-safety lesson. The question “venomous or harmless?” is answered on the identify guide. Here you get one frame from Georgia, four names, and time to train your eye on the atlas catalog.
snakeQuiz.practiceP1: Start with the head. A triangular silhouette from above often recalls a viper; an oval head in profile often belongs to a harmless colubrid. Is the neck clearly narrower than the head, or is it one mass? Many harmless snakes flatten the head and “borrow” that cue in a photo. One frame is not a verdict, but it is a start: if head and neck are separate, look toward colubrids first; if the head is broad and the neck short, compare viper profiles.
snakeQuiz.practiceP2: The pupil, if you can see it. A vertical slit in Georgia often points to a viper; a round pupil often points to a harmless snake. Light changes the cue, and many field photos hide it entirely. If the eye is a blur, do not guess from the pupil alone. Scale sheen is the same trap: a wet grass snake and a dry viper can both look glossy in one crop.
snakeQuiz.practiceP3: Then the pattern. Zigzag, spots, stripes, a plain back — that is what the quiz asks you to see in a second. The Caucasian viper and the grass snake sit close in photographs: both can show a dark back on a pale ground. The split is often head shape, keeled scales, and whether a yellow collar is visible. The smooth snake and the Transcaucasian viper are the same trap at another angle — small, brown, against forest litter.
snakeQuiz.practiceP4: Habitat in the background (stream, rock, steppe, leaf litter) helps, but the quiz does not ask where you are standing. Field safety lives on another page: marks, risk, and what not to do. The job here is speed of the eye — so that before you open a species profile you already know what in the frame caught you. Below are six pairs this atlas confuses most often in photographs.
snakeQuiz.lookalikesTitle: Pairs that confuse a still photo
snakeQuiz.lookalikesLead: This is not field diagnosis. It is what the eye mixes in one frame — and where the quiz draws its distractor names.
snakeQuiz.lookalike1Body: The grass snake often shows a yellow collar and a round pupil; the Caucasian viper a broader head and a vertical pupil when visible. Both are photographed in western forest.
snakeQuiz.lookalike2Body: The dice snake is usually narrower-headed, with strongly keeled scales; the same viper is often shorter, with a sharper zigzag. A stream in the background can belong to either.
snakeQuiz.lookalike3Body: The smooth snake is small, smooth-scaled, round-headed. The Transcaucasian viper sits in the same browns, but the head is broader and the dorsal pattern breaks differently.
snakeQuiz.lookalike4Body: Dinnik’s viper is a high-mountain animal and still matches the smooth snake in size on a photo. Look for head width and the rhythm of the zigzag, not colour alone.
snakeQuiz.lookalike5Body: The Montpellier snake is long and fast, with a large eye; giurza is heavy, with a blunt snout. Size and head profile still split this pair in a photo, unless the crop is tight.
snakeQuiz.lookalike6Body: The glass lizard is a lizard: eyelids and an ear opening. The grass snake has neither. It never appears as a quiz option — it is here so a “snake” in a photo is not always a snake.
snakeQuiz.practiceGuideTitle: Field identification is not this page
snakeQuiz.practiceGuideBody: If you need venomous-versus-harmless logic in the field, that guide stands alone. This quiz only trains you on catalog photos.
